summary.value: The paper introduces GCoT-decoding, a general Chain-of-Thought decoding strategy for LLMs that works on both fixed and open-ended QA tasks. Experiments on six datasets show improved performance and broader applicability over standard CoT-decoding.

strengths.value:
- Overall, the paper is reasonably well-written and includes a sufficient number of ablation studies supporting the proposed approach.

- The investigated scenario is interesting and practically relevant.

- Proposes a general decoding framework that enhances reasoning diversity.

weaknesses.value:
- More details on the computational cost of the proposed approach would be appreciated. 

- [Minor] There is a typo in Figure 1: the label “deocding” appears incorrectly for both the orange and green labels.

- The multi-path exploration process increases decoding time and may limit scalability on large datasets. The paper should better justify or quantify the trade-off between improved reasoning performance and the associated computational cost.

questions.value:
- It is unclear how using the template “so the answer is” directly guides the model toward the desired outcome. Have the authors considered alternative prompting strategies to better investigate this effect?

- Please address the ponts in the weaknesses

comment.value:
### 1.2 Backtracking from local minima (Sec. 3.1) and reliability

> “Similarly, backtracking from local minima (3.1) is interesting and potentially very useful if it works reliably.”

To address the reviewer’s concern about reliability, we have added both quantitative statistics and stronger ablations for the backtracking mechanism, including:
- Add reliability statistics, including:
  - the fraction of questions where backtracking is actually triggered, and
  - among those, the fraction in which backtracking recovers a correct answer that would otherwise be missed.
- Compare against simpler backtracking baselines:
  - no-backtracking (only Fibonacci sampling),
  - random backtracking (random position along the path),
  - and late backtracking (random position within the last L tokens).

| Variant                              | Backtracking trigger rate (%) | Success rate given trigger (%) | MATCH ↑ | BLEU ↑ |
|-------------------------------------|-------------------------------:|--------------------------------:|--------:|-------:|
| No-backtracking (Fibonacci only)    | –                             | –                              | 52.7    | 8.7    |
| Random backtracking                 | 100.0                          | 18.1                           | 52.0    | 8.6    |
| Late backtracking (last *L* tokens) | 100.0                          | 20.4                           | 51.8    | 8.5    |
| Local-minima backtracking (ours)    | 28.0                          | 36.5                           | 54.6    | 9.1    |

On SQuAD v1.1 dev with Gemma-7B, our backtracking mechanism is only triggered on about 28% of questions, i.e., it is not an always-on perturbation. Among these triggered cases, local-minima backtracking successfully recovers a correct answer that the original greedy path would miss in 36.5% of the instances, leading to a net improvement from 52.7 → 54.6 MATCH over the no-backtracking variant.

Random backtracking and late backtracking actually slightly underperform the no-backtracking variant (52.0 and 51.8 vs. 52.7), and their success rates given a trigger (about 18–21%) are substantially lower than that of our local-minima strategy (36.5%). These comparisons clarify that (i) backtracking is only activated when the confidence pattern suggests a local failure, rather than perturbing every path, and (ii) local-minima-based backtracking is significantly more effective than random or late backtracking under the same branching budget.

---

### 1.3 Greedy semantic clustering vs. LLM-based aggregation (Sec. 3.3)

> “Greedy semantic clustering for path aggregation (3.3) similarly seems interesting, but it would be nice to see it compared against simple alternatives, e.g. having an LLM aggregate the paths through prompting.”

Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we implement an LLM-based aggregator that takes the K candidate paths and asks the model to (a) group paths that express the same underlying answer, and then (b) choose a representative answer from these groups. The results on GSM8K and SQuAD v1.1 are shown below:

| Aggregation variant                  | Extra time cost per question (sec.) | GSM8K (Acc., Gemma-7B) | GSM8K (Acc., Mistral-7B) | SQuAD v1.1 (MATCH, Gemma-7B) | SQuAD v1.1 (MATCH, LLaMA-3.1-8B) |
|--------------------------------------|-----------------------------------:|------------------------:|--------------------------:|------------------------------:|----------------------------------:|
| Greedy semantic clustering (ours)    | **0.2**                            | 21.8                   | 18.0                     | 54.6                         | 67.2                             |
| LLM-based aggregation | **8.3**                            | 22.1                   | 19.3                     | 55.8                         | 68.0                             |

As the Table shows, the LLM-based aggregation is indeed a competitive upper bound: it yields slightly higher accuracy/MATCH than our clustering-based method. However, this comes at the cost of an additional 8.3 seconds of processing time per question, making it significantly more expensive in terms of computational resources. Additionally, we observe that the performance of the LLM aggregator is sensitive to the exact phrasing and length of the aggregation prompt.

These comparisons highlight the intended trade-off: while LLM-based aggregation can be marginally stronger, our clustering-based method reaches similar accuracy in a far more compute-efficient and robust way.

## Q3: Stability of LCS-based scoring with repeated answers / punctuation
> For LCS(gen1, gen2) you score only the terminal aligned segment. If the answer phrase appears multiple times, or if tokenization/punctuation differs slightly, could this introduce instability in the confidence calculation?

- **Multiple occurrences of the answer phrase.**  
  To check whether scoring only the terminal segment could be inferior to averaging over all occurrences, we ran a small ablation where we compare:
  1. **SpanAlign (Last):** our default, which uses the terminal LCS-aligned segment, and  
  2. **SpanAlign (Mean):** an alternative that averages the confidence over all aligned segments.
| Method                              | GSM8K (Mistral-7B) | GSM8K (Gemma-7B) | GSM8K (Llama-3.1-8B) | MultiArith (Mistral-7B) | MultiArith (Gemma-7B) | MultiArith (Llama-3.1-8B) | Sports (Mistral-7B) | Sports (Gemma-7B) | Sports (Llama-3.1-8B) |
|-------------------------------------|--------------------:|------------------:|----------------------:|-------------------------:|-----------------------:|---------------------------:|---------------------:|-------------------:|------------------------:|
| GCoT-decoding + SpanAlign (Last)   | 10.7               | 15.4             | 34.0                  | 16.8                    | 19.7                  | 69.3                      | 48.0                | 67.2              | 52.0                   |
| GCoT-decoding + SpanAlign (Mean)   | 10.2               | 14.9             | 33.5                  | 16.1                    | 19.0                  | 68.5                      | 47.1                | 66.3              | 51.4                   |

  This suggests that, when answers may be mentioned multiple times, using the final occurrence is at least as reliable—and often slightly better—than averaging over all mentions.
- **Tokenization and punctuation differences.**  
  We agree that naive LCS alignment could in principle be sensitive to tokenization and punctuation mismatches. To mitigate this, before computing LCS we already normalize both generations by lowercasing them and stripping pure punctuation tokens. This normalization greatly reduces sensitivity to minor tokenization and punctuation differences in practice.

> **Q1:** *“I am confused exactly what +SpanAlign refers to in the tables / figures.”*

We apologize for the ambiguity. In our current manuscript, **“+SpanAlign” refers exactly to the answer-span alignment scoring method described in Sec. 3.2 and Eq. (7)** (the LCS-based alignment between two generations). Concretely:

- Sec. 3.2 defines an alignment method that finds the **longest common subsequence (LCS)** between two generations `gen₁` and `gen₂`, and then computes an answer-span score `Δ_{k,answer}` by averaging the confidence differences along the aligned answer segment (Eq. (7)).
- The **“GCoT + SpanAlign”** variant keeps the *same* path generation, backtracking, and aggregation as our default GCoT-decoding, but **replaces the default length-aware path confidence with this LCS-based answer confidence `Δ_{k,answer}`** when scoring and selecting paths.

In the revision, we will make this explicit by:

1. Renaming the variant in tables/figures to something like **“GCoT + SpanAlign (Eq. 7 answer-span scoring)”**, and  
2. Adding a sentence at the end of Sec. 3.2 stating that *“In our experiments, the ‘+SpanAlign’ variant denotes GCoT-decoding where the path confidence is computed using the answer-span alignment score `Δ_{k,answer}` in Eq. (7).”*

> **Q2:** *“Minor: typo in Figure 1: ‘Cot-deocding’.”*

We will correct the typo in Figure 1 to “CoT-decoding” in the revised version.

title.value: Clarifying the Roles and Relative Importance of GCoT-Decoding Components

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for revisiting our work and raising the score. We understand the remaining concern that the method contains several components and that their relative importance was not clearly delineated. In the revised version, **we have rewritten the ablation section (blue text in Sec. 4.4)** to focus explicitly on the three core modules of GCoT-decoding—Fibonacci-based path generation, local-minimum backtracking, and greedy semantic aggregation—and to quantify each module’s contribution.

**1. Main gains: path generation and aggregation**

First, Tab. 6 shows that the combination of **Fibonacci seeding with “one-step diversification + greedy rollout”** is crucial. Under a fixed path budget of $K{=}10$ (with backtracking and aggregation held fixed), replacing our scheme with standard top-$k$/top-$p$/temperature sampling reduces GSM8K accuracy from about 22%/18% to roughly 8–10%/6–8%, and lowers SQuAD v1.1 MATCH by 10–20 points.

Second, Tab. 8 shows that moving from the MaxPath baseline (no aggregation) to our greedy semantic clustering significantly boosts GSM8K and SQuAD performance while adding almost no extra decoding time. Together, these two components account for the majority of GCoT’s performance gains.

**2. Local-minimum backtracking: a finer-grained improvement**

By contrast, Tab. 7 shows that local-minimum backtracking acts as a smaller but reliable refinement. On SQuAD v1.1 (Gemma-7B), it is triggered on only about 28% of questions, yet still improves MATCH over the no-backtracking variant. Random or late backtracking, which are applied on all questions, slightly harm performance instead.

**3. Conclusion and component hierarchy**

In summary, the new ablations clarify the component hierarchy:

(i) Fibonacci-based multi-path exploration and  
(ii) greedy clustering provide the main performance improvements, while  
(iii) local-minimum backtracking adds a moderate but consistent benefit on top of these core components.

title.value: Follow-up on clarity and robustness concerns

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer,

Thank you again for your thoughtful review and for highlighting both the strengths and weaknesses of our work. We have posted a detailed response addressing your comments on:

- **W1 (clarity in the introductory sections)** – in the revised version, we have already added a more concrete illustration in Section 1, using one math-style example and one free-form QA example to make the core ideas and failure modes of standard CoT decoding more intuitive and easier to follow.
- **W2 (robustness of greedy semantic clustering)** – we clarified the conservative design choices (high similarity threshold, viewing clustering as a low-risk enhancement over MaxPath), and added an embedding ablation (MiniLM / MPNet / E5-small) showing that performance is quite stable across different embedding models.

We also responded in detail to your **Questions Q1–Q3** about:

- the “last numeric token” heuristic and its role beyond math QA,
- the design choice of single-shot backtracking and its trade-off with multi-backtracking variants, and
- the stability of the LCS-based confidence scoring when answers are repeated or tokenization/punctuation differ, including a comparison between “SpanAlign (Last)” and “SpanAlign (Mean)” and a note on our normalization steps.

If you have a moment, we would greatly appreciate it if you could let us know whether these clarifications and additional experiments address your main concerns, or if there are remaining aspects you feel are still insufficiently justified. Any further guidance would be very helpful for us in improving the paper.

Thank you again for your time and careful reviewing.

## W2: Minor typo in Figure 1
> There is a typo in Figure 1: the label “deocding” appears incorrectly for both the orange and green labels.

Thank you for catching this. We will fix the typo in Figure 1 by correcting “Cot-deocding” to “CoT-decoding”.

---

## Q1: Effect of the “So the answer is” template and alternative prompting strategies
> It is unclear how using the template ‘so the answer is’ directly guides the model toward the desired outcome...

We appreciate this question and would like to offer clarification here:

- **In the analysis of standard CoT-decoding (Section 2.1)**, we deliberately use a template such as “So the answer is …” as an *answer-span marker* to illustrate that CoT-decoding is highly sensitive to how the final answer span is defined. When we restrict evaluation to the tokens generated after this marker, small changes in the template or the exact span can cause large swings in accuracy. This is used as a *diagnostic* to motivate our method, not as part of GCoT-decoding itself.

- **In the GCoT-decoding procedure (Section 3)**, the same style of template plays a much more limited role: it is used only as a *post-hoc answer extractor* after the model has already produced a full CoT reasoning path. Concretely, the model first generates the complete reasoning, and only then we append a short continuation prompt  to obtain a concise answer segment which we use for scoring and aggregation. This template does not influence how the reasoning paths are generated, nor does GCoT rely on a specific wording of this phrase; any short, neutral marker that elicits a final answer would suffice.

To address the reviewer’s question more directly, we conducted a small ablation on SQuAD v1.1, where we replaced “So the answer is” with several semantically equivalent templates. As shown in the table, GCoT-decoding’s accuracy remains essentially unchanged across these variants:

| Template                            | SQuAD v1.1 (MATCH, Gemma-7B) |
|-------------------------------------|---------------------:|
| “So the answer is …”      | 54.6                 |
| “Therefore, the answer is …”        | 54.5                 |
| “Final answer:”                     | 54.3               |

The variation across templates is within 0.3 absolute points, which is negligible compared to the gains obtained by switching from greedy / vanilla CoT-decoding to GCoT on the same benchmark. This supports our claim that GCoT does *not* hinge on a specific wording of the template.

### 1.4 Depth of ablation and connections to prompt ensembling (ToT, modern self-consistency)

> “Though the authors show a shallow ablation of some pieces of the method in Table 5, it would be nice to see comparisons to baseline methods for each of these steps … The main comparisons too seem to be missing comparisons to baseline methods for prompt ensembling when computing answers, as many variations have been proposed as early as tree of thought and modern variations of self consistency.”

We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. Together with the expanded baselines for sampling, backtracking, and aggregation in **response 1.1–1.3**, we hope that these additional experimental results will address the reviewer’s concern that our original Table 5 only provided a shallow ablation of some components.

Regarding the broader family of prompt-ensembling methods, as noted in lines 275–276 of the paper: "we do not include prompt-based methods as baselines, as they are orthogonal to GCoT-decoding and can be freely combined (see Section 4.3 for discussion)”. For this reason, in the main text we use self-consistency, CoT-decoding, and standard decoding strategies as our primary baselines, while treating CoT-style prompting itself as an orthogonal component that can be freely combined with GCoT-decoding (see Sec. 4.3), following earlier work such[1] rather than comparing against most prompt-ensembling variants.

---

## W2: Evaluation setup for the models

> “A second major weakness is in the evaluation setup for the models …”

We agree that our current setup can be made more standard and transparent, and we will revise both the prompting and the choice of models accordingly.

---

### 2.1 Low CoT scores on SQuAD and prompting setup

> “Performance for benchmarks like SQuAD is oddly low for these models (e.g. see Figure 3; LLaMA-3.1 8B gets <20% Match score with CoT). This seems like there may be an issue with the baseline method the authors use to query the models.”

Our current protocol uses a relatively simple answer extraction scheme: after the reasoning, we append “So the answer is:” and then post-process the generated text to obtain the final answer. This can lead to noisy answer spans and underestimation of the model’s true capability.

To address this, we will:
- Switch to a more standard, structured answer format on SQuAD and similar datasets, such as:
  - JSON output with a fixed `{"answer": "..."}` field, or
  - explicit tags like `<answer>...</answer>`.
- Update the evaluation scripts so that only the content within the JSON field / tags is used as the predicted answer, eliminating ambiguity from extraneous text.
- Add a small prompt-sensitivity analysis in the appendix, comparing the current “So the answer is:” setup with the structured formats.

---

### 2.2 Answer formatting (“So the answer is:”) vs JSON/tags

> “Similarly, in querying the model to output an answer (e.g. in Sec 2.1), the authors append 'So the answer is: ' at the end of the prompt, although a more standard prompt might begin by asking the model to output answer in a particular format (e.g. in JSON or using tags.”

This is closely related to the previous point. We appreciate the suggestion and will adjust our answer format according to 2.1.

### 2.3 Results on reasoning-tuned models

> “It would be nice also to see results for some reasoning models, where querying for an answer is more straightforward.”

We agree that reasoning-tuned models provide a useful sanity check, as they often come with recommended prompts and answer formats. We added an extra experiment on GSM8K with a reasoning-tuned model DeepSeek-R1:

| Decoding strategy                         | GSM8K Acc. (DeepSeek-R1) |
|-------------------------------------------|--------------------------:|
| Temperature sampling (T=0.7)| 96.1                      |
| Self-consistency (k = 10)   | 96.4                      |
| CoT-decoding (K = 10)                     | 97.2                      |
| GCoT-decoding (K = 10)             | 99.0                      

Even on this near-saturated math benchmark, where a simple temperature-sampling baseline already reaches 96.1% accuracy, GCoT-decoding still provides a consistent margin over CoT and self-consistency. This shows that our method remains beneficial on top of strong reasoning-tuned training rather than relying on weaknesses of smaller, less capable models.

We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and the constructive comments. Below we address the concerns about computational cost, scalability, and the prompting template, and we will also fix the minor typo.

---

## W1 & W3: Computational cost and scalability of GCoT-decoding
> More details on the computational cost of the proposed approach would be appreciated... The multi-path exploration process increases decoding time and may limit scalability on large datasets. The paper should better justify or quantify the trade-off between improved reasoning performance and the associated computational cost.

We agree that it is important to clearly explain the computational trade-off of GCoT-decoding. Our paper already provides a first analysis in Figure 4(b)–(c): as we increase the path budget \(k\), (i) performance improves quickly at small \(k\) and then saturates, and (ii) the decoding time grows approximately linearly in \(k\), with a clear “elbow” around \(k \in [3,5]\) where most of the gains are realized while marginal returns diminish. In practice, this means that for moderate \(k\), GCoT operates within a similar cost range as standard CoT-decoding or self-consistency, but yields consistently better accuracy.

Conceptually, the main cost driver for all multi-path decoding methods (self-consistency, CoT-decoding, and ours) is the number of LLM forward passes times the sequence length. In our case, GCoT-decoding has two stages:

- a **divergence-aware exploration stage** that samples \(k\) reasoning paths using Fibonacci-style branching and local-min backtracking; and  
- a **selection / aggregation stage** that evaluates and clusters the final answers before picking the best one.

The first stage dominates the cost and is comparable to standard CoT-decoding with \(k\) sampled paths, since both require roughly \(k\) full CoT generations. The second stage is much cheaper in practice, as it operates only on short answer segments for computing logit-based scores and sentence embeddings rather than re-querying the LLM. On our open-ended QA benchmarks with a typical setting of \(k = 10\), GCoT-decoding adds only about 20% wall-clock decoding time on top of standard CoT-decoding, yet yields roughly 20–30 absolute percentage points improvement in answer accuracy over greedy decoding.

Regarding scalability on large datasets, we emphasize that GCoT-decoding is a decoding strategy that can be applied selectively and tuned according to budget. The path budget \(k\) and the thresholds used in backtracking can be directly tuned to match a given computational budget, trading off a small drop in accuracy for lower cost if desired.

summary.value: The paper introduces GCoT-Decoding, it is a general chain-of-thought decoding framework designed to uncover deeper correct reasoning paths without relying on predefined output formats. GCoT uses a two-stage branching strategy: (i) Fibonacci sampling to pick diverse early tokens as path seeds, and (ii) backtracking at the first local confidence minimum to spawn corrective branches. Each path is then scored by a top-2 token prob logit gap, length-aware. The final answer is aggregated via "greedy semantic clustering", which accumulates evidence within paraphrase-equivalent answer clusters and selects the representative. Experiments on fixed-answer (GSM8K, MultiArith, BBH-Sports) and free-form (SQuAD, BARQA, Auto-Categorization) QA show GCoT is competitive with standard multi-path decoders on fixed tasks and  improves BLEU/MATCH on free-form tasks; it also composes well with few-shot CoT prompting. Ablations confirm that all three components—branching & backtracking, length×top-2 scoring, and semantic aggregation—are jointly necessary.

strengths.value:
(1) Exploring decoding strategies beyond greedy decoding to cover greater hypothesis diversity makes sense, since the correct reasoning path is often not prominent early in decoding.

(2) The evaluation is carefully executed, with a systematic comparison of multiple decoding strategies.

weaknesses.value:
(1) In the introductory sections, it may be easier to follow if more concrete examples can be added to make the concepts crisper and easier to follow.

(2) Section 3.3 (“Greedy Semantic Clustering for Path Aggregation”) appears potentially fragile, as its behavior can depend heavily on the choice of embedding model.

questions.value:
(1) In Section 2.1’s rule-based extraction, why emphasize taking the last numeric token to compute confidence? Does this mean the analysis of extraction methods’ impact on CoT-decoding was evaluated primarily on math-style fixed-answer QA?

(2) Backtracking is triggered only at the first local minimum below δ, and each path backtracks at most once. Could this single-shot method miss later errors that arise further in the sequence?

(3) For LCS(gen1, gen2) you score only the terminal aligned segment. If the answer phrase appears multiple times, or if tokenization/punctuation differs slightly, could this introduce instability in the confidence calculation?

summary.value: This paper introduces GCoT decoding - a general strategy for decoding by making use of many sampled paths. The method introduces three steps on top of typical decoding, including branching many path (with a fibonacci sampling strategy for diversity), backtracking from local minima (reversing whenever tokens show lower confidence), computing confidence in a length-aware manner, and finally greedy semantic clustering for path aggregation. Compared to standard sampling (greedy, nucleus, beam search) and basic prompting (CoT, self-consistency), it shows some QA improvements for models around the 8B scale.

comment.value:
### 6. Semantic clustering: robustness and LLM-based aggregation

**Concerns (dEkg, 6WEQ):**  
Is clustering fragile to the embedding model? How does it compare to an LLM-based aggregator?

**Revisions**

- **Sec. 3.3** is rewritten to:
  - stress that the most important choice is the **representative answer**, not the clustering algorithm;  
  - explain why, for GCoT, choosing the **earliest-indexed** path per cluster works better than centroid or max-confidence selection;  
  - highlight that we use a **high similarity threshold \(\tau\)** so we only merge clear paraphrases.
- We add an **embedding ablation** in **Appendix G**, summarized briefly in Sec. 3.3, showing that changing the sentence encoder (MiniLM/MPNet/E5) leads to very similar scores; we explicitly note that **GCoT’s clustering is largely insensitive to the specific off-the-shelf embedding** and that this module is **pluggable**.
- We implement an **LLM-based aggregation baseline** and report it in **Sec. 4.4, Table 8** and **Fig. 5 (side table)**:
  - it achieves slightly higher scores than greedy clustering,  
  - but is **much more expensive** per question and sensitive to prompt phrasing.
- We conclude that greedy clustering provides **almost the same accuracy at a fraction of the compute**, aligning with our goal of a **lightweight aggregation module**.

---

### 7. Confidence scoring, LCS alignment, and “+SpanAlign”

**Concerns (98Jy, 6WEQ):**  
What exactly does “+SpanAlign” mean? Is LCS-based scoring unstable with repeated answers or punctuation?

**Revisions**

- **Sec. 3.2** now clearly distinguishes:
  - \( \Delta^{\text{GCoT-decoding}}_{k,\text{answer}} \): the **length-aware logit-gap confidence** used in the main GCoT-decoding, and  
  - \( \Delta^{\text{GCoT+SpanAlign}}_{k,\text{answer}} \): the **LCS-based answer-span score** used in the “+SpanAlign” variant.
- At the end of Sec. 3.2 we add a sentence explicitly stating that **“GCoT + SpanAlign” in all tables/figures uses this Eq. (7) answer-span score for path confidence**, addressing the terminology confusion.
- We specify that, **before computing LCS**, we normalize both generations by **lowercasing and stripping pure punctuation tokens** to reduce sensitivity to tokenization/punctuation.
- We add a **SpanAlign Last vs. Mean** ablation in **Appendix H**, summarized in Sec. 3.2, showing that using the **final aligned occurrence** of the answer is at least as reliable as averaging over all aligned segments, and often slightly better.

---

### 8. Computational cost, scalability, and path budget

**Concern (98Jy):** GCoT uses multiple paths and aggregation; how expensive is it and how does it scale?

**Revisions**

- **Sec. 4.5 and Fig. 4(b–c)** now explicitly analyze:
  - how performance and wall-clock time change as we vary the **path count \(k\)**,  
  - showing **approximately linear** cost growth and **diminishing marginal gains**, with a clear elbow around \(k \approx 3–5\).
- We clarify that:
  - the **main cost** is the number of full CoT generations (shared with self-consistency / CoT-decoding),  
  - scoring and clustering operate only on short answer segments and embeddings, so their overhead is small.
- We emphasize that GCoT-decoding is **budget-tunable**: \(k\) and backtracking thresholds can be set to match a desired cost–performance trade-off.

---

### 9. Evaluation setup, reasoning-tuned models, and relation to prompt ensembling

**Concerns (98Jy, 6WEQ):**  
- Baseline SQuAD results and answer formats should be more standard.  
- How does GCoT perform on reasoning-tuned models?

## Q1: “Last numeric token” in Section 2.1 and math-style QA
> In Section 2.1’s rule-based extraction, why emphasize taking the last numeric token to compute confidence? Does this mean the analysis of extraction methods’ impact on CoT-decoding was evaluated primarily on math-style fixed-answer QA?

First, the “last numeric token” heuristic is deliberately tailored to math-style fixed-answer QA (e.g., GSM8K, MultiArith). In such datasets, the solution trace typically contains intermediate numbers (partial sums, products, etc.), while the *final* answer is presented as the last numeric span in the explanation. This convention is also consistent with the official evaluation scripts and prior CoT work on these benchmarks. Using the last numeric token therefore:

- avoids incorrectly treating intermediate computations as answers, and  
- provides a simple and deterministic mapping from a full reasoning trace to a scalar prediction (and a corresponding confidence score).

Second, our broader claim is **not** limited to math QA: the sensitivity of CoT decoding to the extraction rule also appears on other fixed-answer tasks. For example, on the BBH “Sports Understanding” task (a fixed-label classification setting), we observe clear differences between rule-based extraction and a prompt-based extraction. A small ablation shows that replacing the rule-based extractor with a prompt-based one typically leads to a noticeable drop in accuracy across different models.
| Method                       | Mistral-7B | Gemma-7B | Llama-3.1-8B |
|-----------------------------|-----------:|---------:|-------------:|
| CoT-decoding + rule-based   | 50.6       | 68.4     | 51.0         |
| CoT-decoding + prompt-based | 41.9       | 56.1     | 45.3         |

This supports our main takeaway that how the final answer is extracted from a reasoning trace can have a non-trivial impact on CoT-decoding, even beyond numeric math problems.

## Q2: Single-shot backtracking and later errors
> Backtracking is triggered only at the first local minimum below δ, and each path backtracks at most once. Could this single-shot method miss later errors that arise further in the sequence?

This is an excellent question. In principle, errors can indeed arise later in the sequence. Our choice to backtrack only once at the first local confidence minimum is motivated by two considerations:

- **Empirical structure of CoT errors.** In our qualitative analysis (Table 6), we observe that when a path heads toward an incorrect answer, the earliest few “turning points” (e.g., misclassifying a player’s role in the sports example) already manifest as sharp local drops in token-level confidence. Once the path commits to such a wrong semantic direction, later tokens mostly elaborate on that misconception. In these cases, backtracking at the *first* confidence valley is typically sufficient to redirect the reasoning towards a different, potentially correct branch.
- **Efficiency and path budget.** Allowing multiple backtracking points per path under a fixed path budget significantly increases computational cost and complicates branch allocation (how to trade off early vs. late corrections). We thus adopt a simple one-shot backtracking rule as a pragmatic balance between accuracy and efficiency.

In the revised version, we will make this rationale explicit and, if space permits, add a small ablation where we allow up to more backtracking points per path. 
| Backtracking design      | GSM8K (Acc., Gemma-7B) | GSM8K (Acc., Mistral-7B) | SQuAD v1.1 (MATCH, Gemma-7B) | SQuAD v1.1 (MATCH, Llama-3.1-8B) |
|--------------------------|-----------------------:|--------------------------:|------------------------------:|----------------------------------:|
| 1-back (ours, default)   | 21.8      | 18.0          | 54.6             | 67.2              |
| 2-back (multi-backtrack) | 22.1          | 18.3           | 55.1                 | 67.8                   |
| 3-back (multi-backtrack) | 21.0          | 18.5           | 54.9                 | 66.5                   |

Our preliminary experiments suggest that this multi-backtracking variant yields at most marginal additional gains, while being substantially more expensive, which supports our choice of a single-shot backtracking mechanism as a reasonable efficiency–performance trade-off.

## W2: Robustness of semantic clustering (Section 3.3)
> Section 3.3 (“Greedy Semantic Clustering for Path Aggregation”) appears potentially fragile, as its behavior can depend heavily on the choice of embedding model.

We share the concern that any semantic clustering scheme can in principle be sensitive to the underlying embedding space. Our design of Section 3.3 is intentionally conservative to mitigate such fragility:

- We only merge paths when their cosine similarity exceeds a relatively high threshold (τ), so clusters capture *obvious* paraphrases (e.g., “the war in 1914–1918” vs. “World War I”) rather than marginal semantic similarities.
- Our ablations (Table 9) in the current version already show that the choice of *aggregation rule* (e.g., max-path vs. greedy clustering) has a more pronounced impact than the choice of clustering algorithm, and that GCoT never performs dramatically worse than a simple max-path selection under the same path budget.

### 1.1 Fibonacci sampling (Sec. 3.1) and its alternatives

> “The fibonacci sampling (3.1) seems useful but somewhat arbitrary compared to more standard solutions such as sampling uniformly within a top-p.”

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to more clearly position our Fibonacci sampling relative to standard sampling schemes such as top-p / top-k / temperature sampling. Our design goal is fundamentally different from the usual objective of these methods.

Standard top-p / top-k / temperature sampling performs stochastic sampling at every decoding step, with the primary goal of increasing output diversity across complete sequences. In contrast, our Fibonacci strategy only samples the very first token and then performs pure greedy decoding for the remainder of each path. This “one-step diversification + greedy rollout” follows the spirit of Wang & Zhou on chain-of-thought reasoning without prompting [1]: the aim is not generic diversity, but to unmask reasoning capabilities that are otherwise suppressed by a single greedy trajectory, by exploring a small set of alternative initial reasoning directions and then letting the model deterministically complete each of them.

On top of that, Fibonacci indices are introduced to specifically address the failure mode analyzed in Sec. 2.2: early hypotheses in the ranked list often form clusters of very similar but incorrect reasoning paths, while correct answers can appear relatively later in the index order. Simply taking the first K candidates tends to over-sample a single erroneous cluster. Fibonacci indices provide a simple and deterministic way to spread the sampling budget over the index axis, approximating a log-spaced coverage of the ranked candidates. This avoids over-concentrating on a single early cluster while keeping the number of model calls fixed.

To verify that this design is not arbitrary, we conducted an ablation on the path-generation stage under a fixed budget of K = 10 paths. In all variants, we keep the backtracking and aggregation stages identical, and only change how the K paths are generated:

| Variant                               | GSM8K (Acc., Gemma-7B) | GSM8K (Acc., Mistral-7B) | SQuAD v1.1 (MATCH, Gemma-7B) | SQuAD v1.1 (MATCH, LLaMA-3.1-8B) |
|---------------------------------------|------------------------:|--------------------------:|------------------------------:|----------------------------------:|
| Fibonacci + greedy rollout (ours)     | 21.8                   | 18.0                     | 54.6                         | 67.2                             |
| top-k sampling (k = 10)     | 7.9                    | 6.2                      | 42.1                         | 50.4                             |
| top-p sampling (p = 0.9)    | 8.6                    | 7.0                      | 43.5                         | 51.3                             |
| temperature sampling (T=0.7)| 9.4                    | 7.8                      | 45.0                         | 52.6                             |

As the table shows, when we replace our Fibonacci + greedy rollout with standard step-wise stochastic sampling, performance on GSM8K drops into the 10–15% accuracy range. On SQuAD v1.1, top-k / top-p / temperature sampling also degrades performance by 10–20 MATCH points compared to our method.  

[1] Xuezhi Wang and Denny Zhou, *Chain-of-Thought Reasoning without Prompting*.
